records.statement: The first three Saffire experiments had limited-sized fires and examined ignition and spread over similar materials. Results showed that flames spread quickly and achieved a steady size and burn rate, unlike here on Earth where flames tend to continue to grow. Scientists also learned that the size of the spacecraft had more effect on the fire than anticipated.

sourceLocators.textAnchor: Results showed that flames spread quickly

review.reviewerLabel: Claude (Opus 5.5) in Claude Code, IGNIS event build

records.statement: Results on flame spread in microgravity can be used to establish the rate of heat release in a spacecraft and show that reducing pressure slows down that spread.

records.statement: Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters. Despite these fires, the temperature only increased significantly very near to the fire itself. However, the ambient concentrations of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide rose significantly with the PMMA tests exceeding the 1-hour carbon dioxide limit and the 24-hour carbon monoxide limit.

records.statement: A new phenomenon where a hot flame extinction leads to a low-temperature, “cool-flame” burning in microgravity has been observed for the first time. These cool flames produce partially oxidized fuel and potentially re-ignite to hot flames posing fire safety concerns in spacecraft environments.
